# Aliveville — complete public product brief

Aliveville is a 3D AI world simulator. It is a paused experiment: the hosted game is offline (shut down 2026-09-26) and there is no public play link. It was built to run in the browser and can be run locally from source. It is built by Sarthak Agrawal and published as part of the SaaS Maker software studio.

## Product thesis

Aliveville explores what makes a simulated town feel alive. Its characters are autonomous agents with routines, memories, relationships, dialogue, rumors, and reactions to player actions. The experience combines those systems with quests, combat, world events, and a director system that applies story pressure.

Aliveville is a game simulation, not a general-purpose chatbot or a claim that language models independently control the simulation. Model responses are parsed as structured actions and validated by the game engine before they can affect world state.

## What the experiment contains

The hosted game is offline. The items below describe what the source implements.

- Built to run in a modern browser without installing an application.
- Explore a walkable 3D town.
- Talk to characters whose responses can reflect memory and relationships.
- Encounter quests, confrontations, combat, cutscenes, and changing world mood.
- Use browser-based saves. No public-site account is required.
- Each visitor's live world is isolated in its own session.

## Shipped systems

- Deterministic 3D world generation
- Autonomous agent loop
- Character memory, relationships, reflection, and rumor propagation
- Engine-validated AI dialogue actions
- Real-time melee combat with combos, dodging, lock-on, enemy behavior, and health state
- Quest and story-package systems
- Director-driven villain plans, events, mood changes, and cutscenes
- In-browser WebGPU language-model path with a cloud fallback path
- Text-to-speech and browser speech support
- Browser-local multi-slot saves

## Boundaries

Aliveville does not require an account on its public marketing domain. The experiment is paused; its status may change. Public machine-readable pages intentionally include product facts and policies, not credentials, private operational material, unpublished plans, or user data.
